solutionSource.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

entries.clue: Hold up popular bird at Christmas (5)

blocks.note: to hold up a bank is to rob it

annotation.surface: A festive cheer for the robin, the bird of every Christmas card.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Hold up' reads as 'display' beside a bird; it is the robber's hold-up. The robin is the British Christmas bird, the redbreast on cards.
annotation.definitionFit: The robin is the bird most associated with Christmas in Britain.

entries.clue: After frolic around Kansas, prepares to go home? (7)

indicatorNotes.After: KS is placed after the reversed frolic

annotation.surface: A holidaymaker who has had fun in Kansas starts packing for the journey home.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Around Kansas' looks like travelling about the state; 'around' actually turns the frolic back to front, and 'After' puts KS at the end.
annotation.definitionFit: Someone going home packs their bags again: repacks. The question mark flags this as one example.

entries.clue: Wash black articles (5)

blocks.note: the two English articles, A and THE

annotation.surface: Laundry advice: wash your black items.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Articles' suggests clothing beside 'black' and 'wash'; it means the grammatical articles, a and the.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to bathe something is to wash it, as with a wound.

entries.clue: Writer making one afraid of Christmas? (4,6)

blocks.note: a coward is one who is afraid

annotation.surface: A whimsical question: is there a writer who could make someone scared of Christmas?
annotation.walkthrough: Noël Coward was the English playwright and songwriter; read literally, his name is a person afraid of Christmas.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the author of Private Lives and Blithe Spirit wrote plays, songs and diaries.

entries.clue: Translated from Arabic, one sort of exercise (9)

indicatorNotes.Translated: translating turns words into different forms, so the letters are rearranged

annotation.surface: A phrase translated from Arabic turns out to mean one kind of exercise.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Translated from Arabic' sounds like a language note, but only the letters of ARABIC and ONE matter.
annotation.definitionFit: Anaerobic exercise is short intense effort, such as sprinting or weightlifting.

entries.clue: Hating cereal is out of character (7,3,5)

annotation.surface: Someone who normally loves breakfast suddenly hating cereal is behaving unlike themselves.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface puts 'out of character' about a person's odd breakfast; the phrase is really the definition of the whole answer.
annotation.definitionFit: Something that goes against the grain runs contrary to one's nature.

entries.clue: Scientists in stasis roused to accept award thus (15)

indicatorNotes.roused: stirred up, so the letters of STASIS are mixed
indicatorNotes.to accept: the rearranged STASIS takes in TROPHY and SIC

annotation.surface: Dormant scientists are woken up to go and collect a prize.
annotation.walkthrough: Latin 'sic', familiar from '[sic]' in quotations, means thus. 'Scientists in' looks like part of the picture, but 'in' is only a link.
annotation.definitionFit: Astrophysicists are scientists who study stars and space.

entries.clue: Very odd choice (4)

blocks.note: the adjective: excellent, of the finest quality

annotation.surface: A comment that someone has made a very strange choice.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Choice' reads as a noun, a selection; here it is the adjective meaning fine or excellent, as in 'a rare treat'.
annotation.definitionFit: Rare means uncommon to the point of oddity, and also exceptionally fine, as choice does.

entries.clue: Bishop, getting fit, is shot in part of church (9)

blocks.note: to have a shot is to have a try

annotation.surface: A bishop getting into shape is photographed inside a church.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Getting fit' and 'shot' suggest exercise and photography; they are APT and TRY. The baptistry is where the font stands, used for baptisms.
annotation.definitionFit: A baptistry is the part of a church set aside for baptism.

entries.clue: Bank worker gets sack (7)

blocks.note: the verb: to dismiss in disgrace, especially from the armed forces

annotation.surface: A bank employee is fired.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Sack' reads as a noun, maybe a bag of cash; it is the verb, to dismiss, and cashier has that sense too.
annotation.definitionFit: A cashier handles money in a bank; to cashier someone is to dismiss them in disgrace.

entries.clue: Old man in mine, he can’t work after an hour (15)

indicatorNotes.after: 'after' in its sense of 'following in order', so the work is written down behind the hour

blocks.note: a coal mine is a pit

annotation.surface: An old miner, past his shift, laments that he can no longer work.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Old man' is not an elderly man but a very old kind of man: Pithecanthropus is the former name of Java Man, an early human.
annotation.definitionFit: Pithecanthropus, the 'ape-man', is an early human ancestor, so an old man in the prehistoric sense.

entries.clue: Volume changes, namely by finale in adapted score (10)

indicatorNotes.by: 'by' in its sense of 'next to', so namely stands right beside the finale
indicatorNotes.in: SC END goes inside the rearranged SCORE
indicatorNotes.adapted: changed, so the letters of SCORE are rearranged

annotation.surface: A musical score is reworked so that its volume shifts, especially in the finale.
annotation.walkthrough: SC, short for Latin scilicet, is used in text to mean namely. The musical surface hides that 'score' is only letters.
annotation.definitionFit: A musical term used as a plain definition: each one is a gradual swell in loudness, a change of volume.

entries.clue: Note short skirt (4)

indicatorNotes.short: cut short, so MINIM loses its last letter

blocks.note: a minim is a musical note (a half note); 'short' docks its final M

annotation.surface: A reminder to notice a skirt's short length.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Short skirt' looks like a phrase describing the answer; 'short' belongs with 'Note' and cuts MINIM down.
annotation.definitionFit: A shortened word: the answer is the everyday clipping of miniskirt, the 1960s fashion.

entries.clue: One seeking water wings or odd flaps (7,3)

indicatorNotes.flaps: a flap is a commotion, so the letters are thrown about

annotation.surface: A bird looking for water, flapping its wings or doing something odd.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Water wings' leaps out as the armbands for swimmers, but the definition stops at 'water'; 'flaps' is the verb that stirs the letters.
annotation.definitionFit: A dowsing rod is the forked stick a dowser uses to seek underground water.

entries.clue: Blubber — from whales, obviously (3)

indicatorNotes.from: the answer is taken from inside the words that follow

annotation.surface: Blubber comes from whales, which goes without saying.
annotation.walkthrough: Blubber is whale fat in the surface, but here it is the verb, to cry noisily.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, as verbs: to blubber is to weep noisily and without restraint.

entries.clue: Much food and drink, but not a place to sit (9)

indicatorNotes.not a: tells you to remove an A from TEA

blocks.note: a banquet is a lavish meal

annotation.surface: A feast with lots to eat and drink but nowhere to sit down.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Not a place to sit' reads as a complaint; split it, 'not a' strips TEA and 'place to sit' is the definition. A banquette is an upholstered bench seat.
annotation.definitionFit: A banquette is a long cushioned bench, especially along a wall in a restaurant.

entries.clue: Who, say, follows what, say, magician? (5,6)

indicatorNotes.follows: 'follows' in its sense of 'comes after in sequence', so the Who example goes second
indicatorNotes.what, say: 'say' asks for a sound: WHICH, a word for what, is spoken as WITCH

blocks.note: which = what, as in 'which one?'; sounds like WITCH
Doctor Who, the TV time traveller: the Doctor is an example of a Who

annotation.surface: A riddle about question words, one following another, that ends in a magician.
annotation.walkthrough: The two 'say's do different jobs: the first means 'for example' (Who, the BBC Doctor), the second means spoken aloud.
annotation.definitionFit: A near synonym: the healer of some traditional societies is credited with magic powers, so a kind of magician.

entries.clue: No Christmas crackers for fans of the royals (11)

indicatorNotes.crackers: crackers means crazy, so the letters go wild

annotation.surface: Royalists are denied Christmas crackers, the paper tubes that bang at dinner.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Christmas crackers' is a British table tradition, but here 'crackers' means crazy and scrambles NO CHRISTMAS.
annotation.definitionFit: A loose paraphrase: supporters of kingship as a system are, in practice, fans of the royal family.

entries.clue: Can East in West show? (7)

indicatorNotes.in: TIN E is placed inside MAE

annotation.surface: A question about whether an eastern act can play in the West.
annotation.walkthrough: 'East' and 'West' look like a matching pair of compass points; only East is. West is Mae West, the Hollywood star, whose first name wraps TIN E.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by genus: an afternoon performance at a theatre or cinema is one kind of show.

entries.clue: The old soldier’s first, of course (3)

indicatorNotes.first: take only the first letter of soldier

blocks.note: ye = the, in old spelling ('Ye Olde Shoppe')

annotation.surface: Of course the veteran soldier came first.
annotation.walkthrough: 'The old soldier' reads as a veteran; the phrase splits into 'The old' (YE) and the soldier's first letter.
annotation.definitionFit: 'Of course!' and 'Yes!' are both emphatic agreement.

entries.clue: That entered after coming out (7)

blocks.note: the surface reads a door or room, somewhere physically walked into; the setter means a social world one joins
not leaving a place: 'coming out' is a debutante's formal presentation to fashionable circles

annotation.surface: Something paradoxically entered only after leaving.
annotation.walkthrough: A debutante's 'coming out' was her formal introduction to fashionable society, so coming out is how one enters it.
annotation.definitionFit: High society is what a debutante joins when she comes out.

entries.clue: So good to escape gangsters (4)

indicatorNotes.to escape: to escape is to get out, so the good letter leaves the gangsters

annotation.surface: Relief that the good guy has got away from the mobsters.
annotation.walkthrough: 'So good' reads as praise; 'So' is the definition, alone at the front.
annotation.definitionFit: Thus and so both mean 'therefore' or 'in this way'.

entries.clue: Tipsy concierge drinking Tango in vain (10)

indicatorNotes.Tipsy: drunk, so the letters of CONCIERGE stagger into a new order
indicatorNotes.drinking: the rearranged letters take in T

annotation.surface: A drunk hotel porter sipping a Tango, an orange fizzy drink, to no purpose.
annotation.walkthrough: 'In vain' reads as 'uselessly'; 'in' is only a link and 'vain' the definition. Tango is also a British soft drink, which makes 'drinking' fit.
annotation.definitionFit: Egocentric means self-centred, close to vain.

entries.clue: Power shower, you might say? (5)

indicatorNotes.you might say: points to how the word is spoken

annotation.surface: A power shower, the strong kind in a bathroom.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Power shower' is a bathroom fitting; split it, and 'Power' is the definition and 'shower' the rain.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, as nouns or verbs: royal rule is sovereign power, and to rule is to hold power.

entries.clue: Post-punk fan caught with heroin (4)

annotation.surface: A post-punk music fan is arrested with drugs.
annotation.walkthrough: Goth grew out of post-punk music in the early 1980s, and its fans are goths.
annotation.definitionFit: A goth is a follower of the gothic rock scene that came out of post-punk.

entries.clue: 1950s Britain saw this state funeral? (8,7)

blocks.note: compulsory military service ran in Britain until 1960
a funeral service held by the nation

annotation.surface: A history question about a grand state funeral in postwar Britain.
annotation.walkthrough: National Service was Britain's peacetime conscription, ending in 1960. The question mark marks the second sense as whimsical: a state funeral is a service for the nation.
annotation.definitionFit: National Service is the name for British conscription, which young men served through the 1950s.

entries.clue: Footballer backing county they never forget (9)

indicatorNotes.backing: going backwards, so PELE is reversed

blocks.note: Hants is the abbreviation for Hampshire, an English county

annotation.surface: A footballer loyally supporting his county's fans, who never forget.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Backing' reads as supporting; it reverses PELE. Hants for Hampshire comes from its old name, Hantescire.
annotation.definitionFit: The saying goes that an elephant never forgets.

entries.clue: Capital letters dyslexic starts with (5)

indicatorNotes.starts: the letters at the start of dyslexic

blocks.note: the first of the two letters that open dyslexic
'with' = and, joining the two letters, written out as a word
the second of the opening pair, dy-

annotation.surface: Upper-case letters that someone with dyslexia begins with.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Capital letters' reads as upper case; 'Capital' alone is the definition, the old British 'capital!' meaning excellent.
annotation.definitionFit: Capital and dandy are both old-fashioned words for excellent.
